a6479.speech: Reports that a family of six in Malawi’s major cities now needs approximately K910,000 per month to meet basic needs, while the average monthly income remains stuck around K200,000; in its August 2025 Basic Needs Basket notes that low-income households, who form the majority of urban dwellers, are disproportionately affected by increases in the cost of living, and that many households survive on incomes far below the national poverty line of $3.00 a day (approximately K5,250); says the immediate consequences include food insecurity, erosion of household dignity and the adoption of coping mechanisms: “Families are being forced to cut down on meal frequency and dietary diversity, compromising nutrition, especially for children and pregnant women” ; “Even basic hygiene products such as soap and body lotion are becoming unaffordable, lowering living standards” ; “Households are resorting to borrowing, withdrawing children from school, or engaging in unsustainable activities such as charcoal burning, which has long-term environmental consequences.”

a6479.speaker: Centre for Social Concern (CfSC)
a6479.name: Centre for Social Concern (CfSC)
a6479.speech: Believes the current cost of living crisis requires urgent and multi-pronged government action: urges government to stabilise maize prices by strengthening ADMARC’s presence in local markets to counter speculative pricing, proposes expansion of social protection including cash transfers and food aid targeting vulnerable groups, urges enforcement of fair trade practices and monitoring of price manipulation in urban markets, and in the medium term proposes investing in irrigation and climate-smart agriculture: “Support smallholder farmers’ cooperatives with market access and storage facilities to reduce postharvest losses and stabilise supply. Encourage urban agriculture initiatives to improve access to fresh foods for city residents. Improve energy alternatives, making cooking gas and electricity more affordable to reduce reliance on charcoal and relieve household expenditure.”

a6479.speaker: World Bank (Malawi Country Economic Memorandum)
a6479.name: World Bank (Malawi Country Economic Memorandum)
a6479.speech: Notes that only one in 10 Malawians over the age of 15 has a wage or salary paying job.

a6479.speaker: The previous Malawi Congress Party-led government (ousted in September 2025)
a6479.name: The previous Malawi Congress Party-led government (ousted in September 2025)
a6479.speech: Blamed global crises such as Covid, the Russia-Ukraine war, and climate shocks for the economic decline.

a6479.speaker: Marvin Banda, economist
a6479.name: Marvin Banda
a6479.title: economist
a6479.speech: Says because millionaire status is a prerequisite for survival in Malawi in order to feed a family of six, it is a daunting task for many consumers to fulfil, especially considering that the income gap is extremely unfavourable for many Malawians; adds that with the approaching lean season, massive humanitarian assistance will be required; says the saving grace for many comes from the fact that the economy is largely informal, allowing certain structural rigidities to be overcome: “Indeed, Calvo-pricing indicates that wages and salaries are some of the stickiest economic indicators, which only means that as prices continue to increase, the expectation is that salaries will not increase in proportion to these price increases, which is why the informal economy is important as it serves as a tax haven for the struggling Malawian” ; “Most low-income households are unburdened by income tax due to their nature of employment and levels of income, which helps preserve precious purchasing power” ; “Other consumers are reliant on their families, both in Malawi and abroad, who remit portions of their income and the unfair ratio of 1:9 is incredibly burdensome for many. The performance of remittances has been underscored during the past five years as it has been a source of both income and forex.”

a6479.speaker: Marvin Banda, economist
a6479.name: Marvin Banda
a6479.title: economist
a6479.speech: Hopes that productivity will restore confidence: “However, the agricultural sector remains the most viable source for employment and capitalisation” ; “Along with value-added interventions that aim to penetrate the global value chain to provide solace for many [people] in the economy, the sector has the potential of increasing domestic revenues for governments through the multiple tier approach that will see tax-to-GDP ratio increase.”

a6479.speaker: Velli Nyirongo, economist
a6479.name: Velli Nyirongo
a6479.title: economist
a6479.speech: Believes many Malawian low earners are surviving through great resilience and creativity, often relying on informal economic activities to make ends meet; notes that with a family of six now requiring about K910,000 a month in cities such as Blantyre, Lilongwe, Mzuzu and Zomba while the average salary remains around K200,000, formal employment alone is not enough to sustain most households: “Many Malawians are, therefore, turning to the informal sector, engaging in small-scale businesses such as street vending, subsistence farming and casual labour to supplement their income” ; “However, the challenge is that these informal activities often do not generate sufficient income to cover essential needs and, as a result, some individuals may be tempted to resort to illegal practices such as petty corruption or other unethical means simply to survive.”

a6479.speaker: Velli Nyirongo, economist
a6479.name: Velli Nyirongo
a6479.title: economist
a6479.speech: Argues that it is crucial to address the underlying economic pressures; says one practical solution would be to reduce urbanisation by developing satellite cities and towns where the cost of living, particularly for housing, is lower, which would create more balanced economic opportunities and discourage excessive migration to already overburdened cities: “In addition, the government should focus on reducing the cost of living by tackling inflation and increasing the production of essential goods such as food” ; “Strengthening agricultural output, supporting local industries and improving access to affordable basic commodities would significantly enhance the livelihoods of low earners” ; “Ultimately, a combination of strategic urban planning, economic reform and investment in productive sectors would help Malawians live with greater dignity and stability.”

a6505.speaker: Phillip Jamuhuri Mainga, Managing Director of Kenya Railways Corporation
a6505.name: Phillip Jamuhuri Mainga
a6505.title: Managing Director of Kenya Railways Corporation
a6505.speech: According to Mainga, this initiative will lower the cost of doing business.

a6505.speaker: Officials of Uganda Railways Corporation and Kenya Railways Corporation
a6505.name: Officials of Uganda Railways Corporation and Kenya Railways Corporation
a6505.speech: The officials also announced a joint marketing strategy, which will include a unified tariff.

a6866.speaker: Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 3.8 (UN document)
a6866.name: Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) 3.8 (UN document)
a6866.speech: “Achieve UHC, including financial risk protection, access to quality essential health-care services and access to safe, effective, quality and affordable essential medicines and vaccines for all.”

a6866.speaker: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a6866.name: World Health Organisation (WHO)
a6866.speech: According to the WHO, UHC covers the full continuum of essential health services, from health promotion to prevention, treatment, rehabilitation and palliative care.

a6866.speaker: Research from the World Bank and the WHO
a6866.name: Research from the World Bank and the WHO
a6866.speech: indicates that more than half a billion people are pushed into extreme poverty annually due to healthcare expenses.

a6866.speaker: NOI Polls (2024 survey)
a6866.name: NOI Polls (2024 survey)
a6866.speech: only about 19 in 100 Nigerians have health insurance coverage in Africa's most populous country.

a6866.speaker: World Bank
a6866.name: World Bank
a6866.speech: according to the World Bank, Nigeria's out-of-pocket healthcare expenditure stood at over 76 per cent in 2021.

a6866.speaker: Kelechi Ohiri, Director-General of the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA)
a6866.name: Kelechi Ohiri
a6866.title: Director-General of the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA)
a6866.speech: said the country has recorded significant progress in recent years; said that before the enactment of the NHIA in 2022, Nigeria's health insurance coverage stagnated at approximately seven per cent for nearly two decades, largely due to the limited scope of health insurance, which predominantly served the formal sector, leaving the poor and vulnerable underserved; said health insurance coverage has increased from 16.7 million to 19.2 million Nigerians – a 14 per cent growth in about a year ; “The NHIA now aims to address existing gaps by enforcing mandatory health insurance, increasing public awareness, and restoring trust in the system.”

a6866.speaker: Bolanle Faleye, chief of party for the USAID Local Health System Sustainability (LHSS) project
a6866.name: Bolanle Faleye
a6866.title: chief of party for the USAID Local Health System Sustainability (LHSS) project
a6866.speech: acknowledged the progress made through UHC initiatives but emphasised persistent gaps in financial risk protection, equitable healthcare delivery, and access to essential services; highlighted the burden of out-of-pocket payments, which she said should ideally be reduced to no more than 30 per cent of total healthcare spending ; “Out-of-pocket expenses, a key barrier to UHC, remain as high as 76 per cent. This places a significant financial burden on individuals during vulnerable moments.” ; stressed the need to significantly boost health insurance enrolment to meet the 2030 UHC target, emphasising that only about 19 million people are covered under health insurance nationwide – a far cry from the target.

a6866.speaker: Muhammad Pate, Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a6866.name: Muhammad Pate
a6866.title: Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a6866.speech: said over 8,000 primary healthcare centres across the country have benefited from the Basic Health Care Provision Fund; said the BHCPF would receive at least $2.5 billion in pooled and non-pooled financing from 2024 to 2026 to improve the primary health system nationwide; said N260 billion has been set aside to revitalise PHCs nationwide; said N45 billion had already been disbursed through direct facilities to the state ; “Under the PHC 2.0 reform, we have emphasised equity by allocating financial and human resources across over 8,000 primary healthcare centres. Direct facility disbursements totalling N45 billion have been sent to states, reaching our people directly.”

a6866.speaker: Muhammad Pate, Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a6866.name: Muhammad Pate
a6866.title: Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a6866.speech: At the unveiling of the Nigeria Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative, said the quest to achieve UHC and better health for Nigerians requires a multi-sectoral and whole-of-government approach; said the initiative will leverage the BHCPF, in partnership with state governments and development partners, in a transformational Sector-Wide Approach (SWAp) to improve health outcomes, aligning resources with national health priorities, reducing duplication of efforts, and fostering accountability.

a6866.speaker: Muhammad Pate, Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a6866.name: Muhammad Pate
a6866.title: Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare
a6866.speech: In March, disclosed that about 16,000 doctors had left the country in the last five years, noting that Nigeria now has only 55,000 licensed doctors to serve its growing population of over 200 million.

a6866.speaker: Health experts
a6866.name: Health experts
a6866.speech: are optimistic that the sector-wide approach, focusing on collaboration and coordination, will significantly impact the country's health outcomes. ; Health experts believe that achieving UHC by 2030 requires Nigeria to take the lead in financing its health system.

a6866.speaker: Chika Offor, Executive Director of the Vaccine Network for Disease Control (VNDC)
a6866.name: Chika Offor
a6866.title: Executive Director of the Vaccine Network for Disease Control (VNDC)
a6866.speech: said the sector-wide approach is commendable because the government cannot achieve these health objectives alone; said all sectors, including the private sector, must fully engage in the process.

a6866.speaker: Chika Offor, Executive Director of the Vaccine Network for Disease Control (VNDC)
a6866.name: Chika Offor
a6866.title: Executive Director of the Vaccine Network for Disease Control (VNDC)
a6866.speech: said the health sector is underfunded, which is why it is underperforming; noted that the majority of children are still unimmunised because of a lack of adequate funding in the health system ; “As Nigeria approaches the 2030 UHC target, this shortfall in funding continues to undermine efforts to improve life expectancy, reduce maternal and infant mortality rates, and strengthen the nation's overall health infrastructure.”

a6866.speaker: Chika Offor, Executive Director of the Vaccine Network for Disease Control (VNDC)
a6866.name: Chika Offor
a6866.title: Executive Director of the Vaccine Network for Disease Control (VNDC)
a6866.speech: stressed the importance of transitioning from donor-dependent programmes to sustainable, locally financed initiatives ; “By taking the lead in financing its health system, Nigeria would have greater control over its health priorities and resource allocation.” ; said overcoming this dependency will necessitate increased investment in the health sector, strategic partnerships with the private sector, and sustainable funding mechanisms to ensure continuity and resilience in healthcare delivery; added that this shift is essential for achieving UHC, strengthening Nigeria's health sovereignty and ensuring long-term health outcomes are not at the mercy of external decisions.

a6866.speaker: Mohammad Mohammad, president of the Medical and Dental Consultants Association of Nigeria (MDCAN)
a6866.name: Mohammad Mohammad
a6866.title: president of the Medical and Dental Consultants Association of Nigeria (MDCAN)
a6866.speech: said fewer than 10 per cent of PHCs have doctors, and specialist shortages at primary and secondary healthcare levels intensify the crisis; stressed the need for deliberate strategies to retain healthcare workers and incentivise rural postings ; “Out of the 110,000 registered doctors inducted by MDCN, only about 40,000 remain in Nigeria. This uneven distribution increases workloads, leading to burnout and compromising the quality of care.”

a6866.speaker: Recent reports (on health worker migration)
a6866.name: Recent reports (on health worker migration)
a6866.speech: According to recent reports, thousands of healthcare professionals leave Nigeria annually to seek better opportunities abroad.

a6866.speaker: Review of budgetary allocation to the health sector over the last 22 years
a6866.name: Review of budgetary allocation to the health sector over the last 22 years
a6866.speech: revealed that Nigeria has consistently fallen below the 15 per cent benchmark.

a6876.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a6876.name: World Health Organization (WHO)
a6876.speech: issues warning on health service disruptions reported in 70% of its surveyed country offices as a result of sudden suspensions and reductions in official development assistance (ODA) for health; says the findings raise concern for potentially deeper and prolonged effects on health systems and services across the world, especially in vulnerable and fragile settings, and that this requires urgent action and international response ; says that given the rapidly evolving context, WHO will be monitoring the situation over time and will engage the global health community, including partners and donor agencies, to inform urgent response plans to mitigate deepening country impacts and enable greater sustainability.

a6876.speaker: WHO rapid stock take of 108 WHO country offices, March–April 2025 (report)
a6876.name: WHO rapid stock take of 108 WHO country offices
a6876.title: March–April 2025 (report)
a6876.speech: shows that many countries are working to increase or reallocate funding from domestic and alternative external sources to address gaps, but up to 24% of WHO Country Office responses suggest budget cuts are already translating into increased out-of-pocket payments; reports that the suspensions and reductions in ODA are disrupting all health system functions, with the most frequently reported impacts on health emergency preparedness and response (70%), public health surveillance (66%), service provision (58%), humanitarian aid (56%) and the health and care workforce (54%); that health services are being disrupted across the board in at least one third of responding countries; that the nature and scale of service disruptions are comparable to those observed during the peak periods of the COVID-19 pandemic in some settings; that critical shortages of medicines and health products leave one third of responding countries without commodities for major service areas; that the pause in ODA has led to job losses for health and care workers in over half of responding countries; that over 40% of countries experienced disruptions to key information systems; and that 81 of the 108 WHO country offices have expressed the need for support across a broad range of health areas.

a6876.speaker: Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General
a6876.name: Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus
a6876.title: WHO Director-General
a6876.speech: “These results paint a worrying picture about the impact of the sudden and unplanned cuts to aid on the health of millions of people. Although these cuts are a shock, they are also driving an accelerated transition away from aid dependency to a more sustainable self-reliance, based on domestic resources. Many countries are asking for WHO's support, and WHO is working with them to identify and tailor the most effective measures.”

a6876.speaker: WHO (note to editors)
a6876.name: WHO (note to editors)
a6876.speech: states that these findings represent a snapshot of the health systems and health services situation in a rapidly evolving situation; senior WHO country office staff were surveyed over the period of 7 March to 2 April 2025 through a structured survey; WHO country offices in low- and lower-middle-income countries across all six WHO regions were included; and they do not reflect the official views of the governments in the countries, territories and areas.

a6888.speaker: Josef Abramowitz, Gigawatt Global President and Chief Executive Officer
a6888.name: Josef Abramowitz
a6888.title: Gigawatt Global President and Chief Executive Officer
a6888.speech: Disclosed in an interview with the Zambia News and Information (ZANIS) on the sidelines of the Israeli-Zambia Business Forum 2023 in Jerusalem that his company will inject US$100 million in the development of a 71 Megawatt (MW) hybrid solar PV and wind power project in Chibombo.

a6888.speaker: Josef Abramowitz, Gigawatt Global President and Chief Executive Officer
a6888.name: Josef Abramowitz
a6888.title: Gigawatt Global President and Chief Executive Officer
a6888.speech: Said his company is a multinational renewable energy platform that develops, finances, builds and operates utility-scale PV solar projects in emerging markets ; said that based on experience as pioneers of the solar industry in Israel, the company’s founders built the first grid-connected solar project in East Africa, an 8.5mw solar PV plant in Rwanda ; said Gigawatt Global reached financial close on their 8.67mw solar PV project in Burundi in January 2020, with construction now under way.

a6888.speaker: Josef Abramowitz, Gigawatt Global President and Chief Executive Officer
a6888.name: Josef Abramowitz
a6888.title: Gigawatt Global President and Chief Executive Officer
a6888.speech: Said the Chibombo Gigawatt hybrid solar PV and wind project was started in 2018 but the project could not take off due to the challenges that the energy industry has faced through the years: “Plans to start this project in Chibombo started in 2018 but we could not proceed much with project implementation due to a number of road blocks and other challenges faced and now all is well as things are moving smoothly and ready to roll out our project.”

a6888.speaker: Josef Abramowitz, Gigawatt Global President and Chief Executive Officer
a6888.name: Josef Abramowitz
a6888.title: Gigawatt Global President and Chief Executive Officer
a6888.speech: Expressed happiness that the business environment in Zambia has tremendously changed following the change of government ; said Gigawatt Global has since obtained the Investment Licence from Zambia Development Agency (ZDA) and signed an implementation agreement with the Ministry of Energy ; said a number of Grid Impact studies in Topography have already started and that the company will be moving on site to start full project implementation ; thanked the government for making it easy for foreign investors to invest in Zambia ; said his company is ready to work with the Zambian people in the economic development of the country: “Our company is ready to move in and commence the implementation of the project. We have the money and all we are waiting for is to complete all the formalities.”

a6888.speaker: Hakainde Hichilema, President of Zambia
a6888.name: Hakainde Hichilema
a6888.title: President of Zambia
a6888.speech: Called on Israeli investors to consider investing in Zambia, saying Zambia has a conducive business environment to support and promote foreign investment; said this during a State banquet hosted in his honour by the Israeli President, Isaac Herzog, at the presidential residence in Jerusalem.

a6944.speaker: Moussa Alassane Diallo, Malian Minister of Industry and Commerce
a6944.name: Moussa Alassane Diallo
a6944.title: Malian Minister of Industry and Commerce
a6944.speech: Informed the Council of Ministers of Wednesday, July 23 of Mali's participation in the Osaka 2025 World Expo in Japan, whose central theme is "Designing future society, imagining our life of tomorrow"; said the objective of Mali's participation is to promote the supply of Malian goods and services through the planned meetings and business appointments, and that the participation will be an opportunity to strengthen ties of cooperation with Japan and the other participating countries with a view to exploring new modes of economic cooperation.

a6944.speaker: Massoudou Cisse, Director General of Apex-Mali
a6944.name: Massoudou Cisse
a6944.title: Director General of Apex-Mali
a6944.speech: "The Mali-Japan Business Forum is the expression of a shared ambition, turned towards the future."

a7131.speaker: Mary Njoroge, WFP Representative in Djibouti
a7131.name: Mary Njoroge
a7131.title: WFP Representative in Djibouti
a7131.speech: Stressed that this project is proof that it is possible to live with dignity from agriculture in the Republic of Djibouti.

a7131.speaker: Mary Njoroge, WFP Representative in Djibouti
a7131.name: Mary Njoroge
a7131.title: WFP Representative in Djibouti
a7131.speech: She also thanked the Ministry of Agriculture for its collaboration and for the capacity building of the members of the FIIAN agricultural cooperative, as well as for its participation in setting up the solar panel project.

a7131.speaker: Mrs Andrea, Deputy Chief of Mission of the US Embassy in Djibouti
a7131.name: Mrs Andrea
a7131.title: Deputy Chief of Mission of the US Embassy in Djibouti
a7131.speech: Recalled that the United States government is pleased to contribute to the efforts already undertaken by Djibouti's Ministry of Agriculture, and to work in close collaboration with international partners that share the same objectives, such as the European Union, the FAO, and above all WFP, which spared no effort to make this day possible.

a7160.speaker: International Committee of the Red Cross and the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
a7160.name: International Committee of the Red Cross and the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
a7160.speech: According to them, there are over 120 ongoing conflicts worldwide, with more than 310 million people requiring humanitarian assistance.

a7237.speaker: Melusi Masuku, Principal Secretary of the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Trade (Eswatini)
a7237.name: Melusi Masuku
a7237.title: Principal Secretary of the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Trade (Eswatini)
a7237.speech: Emphasised the crucial role of the African Trade Observatory (ATO) in empowering businesses with the necessary trade intelligence to navigate and seize emerging opportunities across the continent; highlighted that the ATO's capacity to provide real-time and reliable data was essential for informed decision-making and strategic planning in the rapidly evolving landscape of African trade.

a7237.speaker: Melusi Masuku, Principal Secretary of the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Trade (Eswatini)
a7237.name: Melusi Masuku
a7237.title: Principal Secretary of the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Trade (Eswatini)
a7237.speech: Pointed out that the inclusion of the trade in services data management component in the second phase of the ATO project was a significant development; expressed gratitude for this support, noting that the lack of detailed and reliable trade data had historically hindered the nation's ability to fully leverage intra-African trade opportunities, particularly in the services sector; noted the growing importance of services in global trade, stating that they constitute a significant portion of the GDP for most African countries, including Eswatini: "In fact, according to the African Development Bank's Country Focus Report of 2024, the services sector contributed approximately 51.3 per cent to Eswatini's GDP in 2023"; however, he noted that the current state of trade in services data remained limited, with only a few countries worldwide providing detailed statistics.

a7237.speaker: African Development Bank, Country Focus Report of 2024
a7237.name: African Development Bank
a7237.title: Country Focus Report of 2024
a7237.speech: Cited by Masuku as the source of the finding that the services sector contributed approximately 51.3 per cent to Eswatini's GDP in 2023.

a7237.speaker: Melusi Masuku, Principal Secretary of the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Trade (Eswatini)
a7237.name: Melusi Masuku
a7237.title: Principal Secretary of the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Trade (Eswatini)
a7237.speech: Commended the ITC (International Trade Centre) and the European Union for their continued technical and financial support to Eswatini; described their contributions as invaluable in striving to create a more integrated and prosperous Africa, what he termed "The Africa we want"; expressed hope that Eswatini would position itself as the Southern African Trade Hub.

a7237.speaker: Melusi Masuku, Principal Secretary of the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Trade (Eswatini)
a7237.name: Melusi Masuku
a7237.title: Principal Secretary of the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Trade (Eswatini)
a7237.speech: Encouraged all participants to work collaboratively to unlock the full potential of trade in services, benefitting not only the people of Eswatini but the entire African continent.

a7403.speaker: Ikeja Viva L'Amour Lions Club
a7403.name: Ikeja Viva L'Amour Lions Club
a7403.speech: Made a clarion call on the government, private organizations and well-meaning individuals to reach out to orphanage homes.

a7403.speaker: Yewande Akapo, Activity Chairperson for the event, Ikeja Viva L'Amour Lions Club
a7403.name: Yewande Akapo
a7403.title: Activity Chairperson for the event, Ikeja Viva L'Amour Lions Club
a7403.speech: Took a swipe at the government as not doing enough for the destitute in the society; said some of the children in the homes were abandoned by parents who have no means of livelihood as well as those subject to abject poverty currently prevalent in the country: “The government should try to alleviate the poverty level, educate children and adults who have missed childhood education. The government should intensify their efforts in caring for the poor, needy, and vulnerable in society. Build more orphanage homes and adequately maintain them. There are more private orphanage homes than government established homes. The government should rise up to their responsibilities. The homes depend on private sponsorship. I'm making a Macedonian Call to organisations, institutions, associations, church societies, and individuals to come over and support these orphanages.”

a7403.speaker: Anastasia Gbem, president, Ikeja Viva L'Amour Lions Club
a7403.name: Anastasia Gbem
a7403.title: president, Ikeja Viva L'Amour Lions Club
a7403.speech: Explaining why the club organised the party for the orphanage home, noted that humanitarian services aimed towards the less privileged in the society is one of the core pillars of service in Lions International Club; admitted that children in the orphanage homes cannot cater for their own basic needs, as a result of which their wellbeing is totally dependent on the goodwill and generosity of well-meaning people in the society: “In line with its goal of providing humanitarian assistance to the needy, Ikeja Viva L'Amour Lions Club has for many years provided help to children in the orphanages just to ensure that their basic needs are met thereby giving them the love and care they desire. Children in the orphanage should not be left alone to suffer or lack basic necessities of life. They need all the support, care and love from the society so that they can grow up to fulfill their dreams in life and become good members of the society.”

a7403.speaker: Nnamdi George, Admin Officer of Little Saints Orphanage
a7403.name: Nnamdi George
a7403.title: Admin Officer of Little Saints Orphanage
a7403.speech: In appreciation, thanked the club for putting smiles on the faces of the children as well as called on Nigerians to keep being a source of blessing to orphanages so as to rid the society of street children and orphans.

a7473.speaker: Erik Habers, head of cooperation at the Delegation of the EU to Ethiopia
a7473.name: Erik Habers
a7473.title: head of cooperation at the Delegation of the EU to Ethiopia
a7473.speech: Said the aid was particularly aimed at the maintenance of the trunk roads leading to the exits of the country: “This support has been ongoing for 25 years” ; “Initially, it was going toward building these roads leading to other regions jointly with the government.”

a7473.speaker: Erik Habers, head of cooperation at the Delegation of the EU to Ethiopia
a7473.name: Erik Habers
a7473.title: head of cooperation at the Delegation of the EU to Ethiopia
a7473.speech: Said that though the release of the funds depends on the achievement of targets set by the government, there was space for negotiations where that was not the case: “There are various reasons why targets may not be achieved. This includes instances that are outside of the government's control.”

a7473.speaker: Johan Borgstam, head of the EU Delegation to Ethiopia
a7473.name: Johan Borgstam
a7473.title: head of the EU Delegation to Ethiopia
a7473.speech: Sees a lack of independent investigations on the numerous claims of human rights abuses coming from Tigray Regional State and widespread ethnic profiling remaining a cause for concern for the EU: “It's in the interest of the government to get independent investigators and forensic experts. It'll be a clear signal for any country that there is nothing to hide.”

a7473.speaker: Ethiopian government
a7473.name: Ethiopian government
a7473.speech: Asserts that it has deployed local independent investigators to the Regional State to examine the circumstances.

a7473.speaker: Dina Mufti, Spokesperson for the Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a7473.name: Dina Mufti
a7473.title: Spokesperson for the Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a7473.speech: Believes all the pre-conditions are already in place: “A humanitarian corridor has been opened. There are modules of operation in place with the UN, and Ethiopia is doing its level best to deliver aid to those in need. We want to nurture and grow the relationship with the European Union. The country is a sovereign state; the EU shouldn't ask of Ethiopia what it doesn't ask of its own countries.” ; mentioned operationalised resettlement schemes in the region along with the work of the interim government as indicators that things are returning to normal.

a7473.speaker: Johan Borgstam, the EU's Envoy in Addis
a7473.name: Johan Borgstam
a7473.title: the EU's Envoy in Addis
a7473.speech: Believes Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's statement on the distinction between members of the TPLF and the people of Tigray could not be understated, but says the EU is concerned by what seems to be the ethnically targeted suspension of non-military personnel from work: “Though the future remains to be seen, this is an important and clear signal. It was made with the hope that Ethiopia will move toward these requests.”

a7473.speaker: Kassahun Berhanu (PhD), professor of political science & international relations at Addis Abeba University
a7473.name: Kassahun Berhanu (PhD)
a7473.title: professor of political science & international relations at Addis Abeba University
a7473.speech: Says that Ethiopia is not a region under the Union and interfering on internal matters of a country is tantamount to questioning the sovereignty of the country, and that humanitarian access should be guaranteed but through government coordination, as it was done in times of peace, let alone war: “This isn't because the EU demands it or not. There needs to be security and peace established by the government now as it goes.”
